how is it; what is it like
grammar: Keep the statement word order and use a rising intonation; the polite present ending stays the same.
omit a subject that is clear from context
Korean often leaves out ‘you’; use a name or title when needed rather than a direct second-person pronoun.
a noun can modify the following noun
The first noun specifies the type or topic of the second, as in 중국어 선생님.
What about N?; a polite contextual follow-up question
Attach 요 to the topic-marked noun: 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel.
all N; place 다 before the predicate
Korean commonly leaves plurality to context rather than marking every noun as plural.
very; a high degree before an adjective
For example, 아주 좋아요 means “very good.”
a little; somewhat before an adjective
For example, 조금 추워요 means “It's a little cold” or “I feel a little cold.”
시간 표현 + 주어 + 동사 / 주어 + 시간 표현 + 동사
A time expression can come before the subject or after it, before the action.
For example, 오늘 저는 요리해요 and 저는 오늘 요리해요.
for a length of time; put 동안 after the duration and before the verb
For example, 오 분 동안 쉬어요. In Korean, the duration phrase comes before the verb.
a little of N; put 조금 after the noun
For example, 밥 조금 주세요 means “A little rice, please.”
Place 전에 after a noun, as in 수업 전에 (before class).
Express a calendar year with a number followed by 년.
Korean reads the complete number by place value: 이천이십육 년, not digit by digit.
Use 번 after a number to identify a numbered item, such as a room.
For example, 삼 번 방 means room number three.
Put 반 after the hour: 여덟 시 반. Use a native Korean numeral before 시.
For possession, mark the possessor with 은/는 and the thing possessed with 이/가: 저는 친구가 있어요.
form eleven to nineteen with native Korean numbers; use the counter forms before counters
For example, 열다섯 권 and 열 시간.
ask how much of something someone does
Use 얼마나 before the verb to ask about an open amount, as in 물을 얼마나 마셔요?
be in front of, behind, or beside N
Korean uses location nouns followed by 에, rather than a location suffix.
Put 뭐, 누구, or 어디 in the part of the sentence being asked about; no extra question particle is needed.
누구 is 누가 when it is the subject.
call N by the name N
For example, 아이를 이 이름으로 불러요.
some N; a few members of a group
몇몇 comes before the noun. Korean often leaves plural marking unspoken when the meaning is clear.
this/these N; that/those N over there
Korean often leaves plural marking unspoken when the meaning is clear. Use 그 for something near the listener or already mentioned.
이 points to something near the speaker; 그 points to something already known or being indicated.
say a quoted word or sentence
Use 너무 before an adjective to express excess or strong emphasis. In an exclamation, the emphasis can come from the wording and intonation.
Place 정말 before an adjective to emphasize an evaluation.
plural marker for people, animals, or things
Attach 들 to a noun to indicate more than one. Korean often leaves the plural unmarked when the meaning is clear.
Use the quoted descriptive clause before 생각하다.
did not V; have not V-ed
Put 안 before a past-tense verb, or use -지 않았어요. For example, 어제 아침을 안 먹었어요 means “I didn’t eat breakfast yesterday.”
For example, 월요일 is Monday and 일요일 is Sunday.
Form hundreds and thousands by placing the number before 백 or 천, then adding any remaining place values.
Korean commonly says 백 원 and 천 원 without 일 before 백 or 천; for example, 이천오백 원 and 육백팔 원.
Ask how big or how much with 얼마나; ask someone's age with 몇 살이에요?
Korean asks “How old?” with 몇 살이에요?, not a literal equivalent of “how big.”
polite title attached after a name
Use 씨 after a person’s name when addressing or referring to them politely; 씨 is not a standalone vocabulary item.
Put 후에 after a noun to say what happens after it.
Ask how an action is done; put 어떻게 before the verb phrase.
use 선생님 after a name as a polite form of address
ask how something is or what it is like
ordinal number: first, second, third, and so on
Put 번째 after a number, as in 첫 번째 책 and 두 번째 책.
Place 어느 before the noun being asked about.
Form month names with a Sino-Korean number before 월
For example, 일월 means January and 이월 means February.
Korean number expressions usually omit zero place values; for example, 1,008 is 천팔.
Unlike Chinese, Korean does not say a zero to bridge skipped place values.
half a unit of something; put 반 before the unit word
For example, 우유 반 컵 means half a cup of milk.
Let's V; a polite informal suggestion
Use 우리 with a polite present-tense verb to make a suggestion.
Read a year as a Sino-Korean number written in Hangul.
Use this for the year-number portion before 년, for example 이천이십육 년.
Use 에 to mark the destination with 도착하다.
the Sino-Korean number two before a larger number unit
Use 이 before 천 to form 이천.
Use 위안 as the currency unit for prices in yuan.
Use 밖 after a noun to refer to its outside; add 에 when marking the location.
Use 밖 after a noun to indicate a location outside it.
twenty minutes, using a Sino-Korean number
Use 이 before 십 to form 이십 (20) in a minute expression.
at, in, or on a place; location of an event or state
Use 에 after a place expression to show where an event occurs or a state applies.
Use 일째 after a number to count the day in a sequence.
Use 에 to mark the place where people or things are; this use is not covered by the taught grammar points.
Use 구 in dates and other Sino-Korean number expressions.
Use Hangul numerals for date numbers, including forms not otherwise listed as vocabulary.
year, month, and day in a date
Express a date in year-month-day order.
Use a number with 월 for the month and a number with 일 for the day.
Use 에 to mark the place where someone lives.
I will; speaker's intention or promise
Use this polite ending when saying what you will do.
Use the first form after a final consonant and the second after a vowel; do not insert a subject when context makes it unnecessary.
The negative copula takes the subject particle on the noun being denied.
as for N; topic or contrast
The topic particle introduces or contrasts a topic; it is not interchangeable with the subject particle in every context.
As for coffee, I like it.
Choose the consonant-final or vowel-final form; new information and identification often use this particle.
Use after an object; it may be omitted in casual conversation but retain it in early controlled practice.
Existence and location use this particle; actions at a place normally use the action-location particle instead.
The book is on the desk.
I am not at home now.
at N; location of an action
Distinguish the place where an action occurs from a destination or location of existence.
I eat lunch at a restaurant.
The particle marks a destination; the motion verb is chosen relative to the conversational viewpoint.
A friend comes to our house.
at N; time of an event
Used with clock times and many calendar expressions, but not normally with today, tomorrow, or yesterday.
The possessive particle is often omitted in speech; humble and familiar possessive pronouns have contracted forms.
I know the name of the school.
The first is common in conversation; the latter pair is frequent in writing and more formal contexts.
I watch a movie with a friend.
This particle often replaces the subject or object particle; other combinations depend on the particle.
Focuses on the noun; compare its scope with a negative sentence when interpreting restrictions.
Vowel harmony and common contractions determine the surface form; descriptive verbs do not need an extra copula.
The past marker attaches to the stem before the polite ending; practice irregular stems as word families.
I was very busy last week.
will; be going to; expected future
Expresses plans or predictions; avoid treating it as a mechanical equivalent of every English future.
I am going to read a book tomorrow.
I will rest on the weekend.
Direct statements usually concern the speaker; ask about the listener's wishes rather than asserting another person's internal state.
I want to go to Korea.
What would you like to eat?
Short negation; for many action nouns with the do-verb, place the negative immediately before the do-verb.
Also has honorific statement uses; context and intonation distinguish requests from descriptions.
Requests a helpful action; do not confuse the auxiliary with giving a physical object.
Attach the prohibition to the verb stem; this is not the ordinary negative statement form.
Please do not take photographs here.
Please do not speak too quickly.
Connects clauses without necessarily asserting a cause; tense is commonly expressed at the final predicate.
저는 책을 읽고 친구는 음악을 들어요.
I read a book, and my friend listens to music.
The room is big and clean.
At this stage teach ordinary explanations; avoid following the causal use with a command or suggestion.
I go to bed early because I am tired.
I am at home because it is raining.
go / come in order to V
The first predicate states the purpose of a motion verb; it is not a general-purpose replacement for all purpose clauses.
I am going to buy a book.
shall we V?; shall I V?
A tentative proposal or offer; predictive question uses are introduced later.
Expresses ability or possibility; the bound noun is written separately.
Teach ongoing action first; resultant-state uses depend on the verb and are introduced later.
I am reading a book now.
I am waiting for a friend.
N that is A; descriptive noun modifier
Descriptive predicates directly modify nouns; the existential adjective family has a different modifier form.
Use native or Sino-Korean numbers according to the counter; native one through four contract before counters.
Honors the subject, not the listener; some common predicates use a special honorific word instead.
The teacher is reading a book.
may V; be allowed to V
Use a question to request permission; descriptive predicates are possible but not the central classroom use.
Expresses necessity; the second auxiliary is frequent in conversation.
I have to do the homework by tomorrow.
I need to go to the hospital.
Expresses intention or a developing situation; introduce first-person plans first.
I plan to travel during the vacation.
I intend to go to bed early today.
N that does / is doing V
The present action modifier differs from the descriptive-verb modifier.
The person going over there is my friend.
The book I am reading is interesting.
N that did / has done V
This action-verb modifier marks completed action; context determines whether English uses past or present perfect.
I called the friend I met yesterday.
Nominalizes a clause; distinguish grammatical nominalization from a concrete thing described by a relative clause.
Often appears in activity labels and fixed evaluative constructions.
This chair is comfortable to sit on.
Places the comparison standard before the particle; the degree word may be omitted.
The train is faster than the bus.
by means of; toward; made of N
Use the vowel form after a vowel or the liquid final consonant; the sense depends on context.
I go to school by bus.
I made a box out of paper.
The first two are ordinary recipient forms; the honorific form respects the recipient, not necessarily the subject.
I sent a letter to a friend.
I asked the teacher a question.
Distributes an event or property over members of a set or intervals.
Food differs from country to country.
Long-form negation is useful in careful speech and writing; apply tense to the final auxiliary.
know / not know how to V
Skill and method use differs from the belief or expectation sense of this same construction.
I know how to ride a bicycle.
I do not know how to use this machine.
Typically combines with suitable intransitive or passive predicates; contrast ongoing-action progressives.
The students are seated on chairs.
in an A way; adverbial manner
Converts a descriptive predicate into an adverbial; fixed lexical adverbs may be more idiomatic for some stems.
